content.title: About
content.content: Black cumin (Nigella sativa), also called black seed or nigella, is an annual plant native to Southwest Asia and the Mediterranean. Its small black seeds have a bitter, peppery flavor with notes of onion, pepper, and oregano. The seeds are added to bread, flatbreads, vegetable dishes, and spice blends, and oil is pressed from them.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black cumin is not true cumin and not the same as cumin seed: they are different plants.
The Latin name Nigella comes from a word meaning black.
The plant is related to buttercups, not to cumin.
The seeds are part of the Indian spice blend panch phoron.
The seeds are often lightly toasted in a dry pan before use to bring out their aroma.

items.title: Contains thymoquinone
items.content: Thymoquinone is a compound with antioxidant properties that is actively studied.

items.title: Contains unsaturated fatty acids
items.content: The seeds and oil contain linoleic acid and other unsaturated fats.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: In small amounts, the seeds provide iron, calcium, and magnesium.

items.title: Studied for effects on blood sugar and pressure
items.content: Some small studies look at effects on blood sugar and blood pressure, but evidence is limited.

items.title: Adds flavor
items.content: A pinch of seeds gives dishes a bold, peppery aroma.

items.title: Pregnancy
items.content: During pregnancy, avoid large amounts of the seeds and oil, and discuss supplements with a doctor.

items.title: Medications
items.content: Black cumin may affect blood sugar and blood pressure and may interact with diabetes medications, blood pressure medications, and anticoagulants.

items.title: Allergy and skin
items.content: Allergy is possible, and the oil can cause contact dermatitis when applied to the skin.

items.title: Supplements and large amounts
items.content: Concentrated supplements and high doses are not well studied; do not exceed the amount on the package.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sprinkle the seeds on bread, flatbreads, and rolls, or add them to lentils, vegetables, salads, marinades, and yogurt. To bring out the aroma, lightly toast them in a dry pan. They can also be ground. Use a pinch, since the flavor is strong and bitter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place and use them within a year. Keep the oil in a dark bottle in a cool place, tightly closed.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken, fried in a coating, consists of pieces of chicken meat covered with breadcrumbs or batter and deep‑fried until golden and crisp. Both the skin and the coating are edible, providing a crunchy texture and rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fried chicken is one of the most popular dishes worldwide and has countless regional variations.
Coatings can include spices, herbs, cheese, nuts or panko, allowing endless flavor combinations.
Chicken meat is high in protein, while the crispy crust adds a pleasant textural contrast.
Traditionally served with sauces such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, or spicy chili.
In some cuisines the chicken is fried in oil infused with aromatics like rosemary or thyme.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Fried chicken supplies niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: High protein and moderate fat content help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Regular consumption combined with exercise can help maintain and build lean muscle.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds calories; people watching their weight should control portion size.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Reusing oil can create trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may have an allergic reaction to chicken proteins.

items.title: Foodborne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella or campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried chicken can be enjoyed on its own, added to salads, sandwiches, wraps, or served with sides such as mashed potatoes, rice, or vegetables. Cut into bite‑size pieces for children.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fried chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: The chicken salad sandwich wrap is a soft wheat tortilla filled with a creamy chicken salad made from boiled chicken breast, mayonnaise, mustard, fresh vegetables, and aromatic herbs. It is a convenient, nutritious snack suitable for lunch, picnics, or a quick dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken salad in the wrap is often mixed with celery and apple for a light sweetness and crunch.
The practice of wrapping salads in thin tortillas originated in the United States in the mid‑20th century as a fast take‑away option.
The tortilla usually contains a small amount of whole grains, boosting its fiber content.
Wraps are easy to cut into bite‑size portions, making them popular in catering.
Variations may replace mayonnaise with a yogurt‑based sauce to lower calories.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using light mayo or yogurt keeps saturated fat levels moderate.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Vegetables in the salad (e.g., carrots, celery) add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Vitamin C from veggies
items.content: Fresh peppers and other vegetables boost the wrap with vitamin C, supporting immunity.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or added ingredients.

items.title: Mayonnaise content
items.content: Traditional mayo increases calories and fat; light versions are recommended for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Chicken must be fully cooked and stored below 4 °C to prevent salmonella growth.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared sauces and seasonings can be high in salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The wrap is easy to eat by hand, preferably cut in half. It can be served cold or gently warmed in a microwave. Pairs well with a light green salad or a fruit juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled wrap in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, separate the tortilla from the salad to prevent sogginess.

content.title: About
content.content: Cream of Rice is a finely milled rice product that turns into a smooth, creamy porridge when cooked. It is gluten‑free, easily digestible, and commonly used in infant nutrition as well as in low‑carb and sports diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream of Rice is made from whole rice grains that are dry‑milled into a fine powder.
It is a popular quick‑carb source for athletes because it provides fast‑acting energy.
Unlike oatmeal, Cream of Rice contains very little fiber, resulting in a very soft texture.
The product dissolves readily in hot water or milk, creating a lump‑free consistency.
It is often added to baby formulas for newborns due to its hypoallergenic nature.

items.title: Fast energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates in Cream of Rice are rapidly absorbed, delivering quick energy useful before workouts or during recovery.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Being gluten‑free and low in fiber, it is gentle on the digestive system, especially for those with sensitivities.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The product contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Supports infant growth
items.content: Its hypoallergenic profile and smooth texture make it an ideal first solid food for babies.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin or gastrointestinal reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cream of Rice has a high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size and pair it with protein or fat.

items.title: Lack of fiber
items.content: The low fiber content can cause a rapid blood‑sugar spike and may lead to hunger soon after eating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prepare Cream of Rice by pouring hot water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage over the powder and stirring until smooth. Sweeten with honey, fruit puree, or add berries, nuts, and protein powder for a more balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Cream of Rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent moisture buildup and mold.

lasagna-with-chicken-or-turkey-and-spina.title: Lasagna with Chicken or Turkey and Spinach

content.title: About
content.content: Lasagna is a classic Italian dish made of layered pasta sheets, sauce, cheese, and filling. This version uses tender chicken or turkey meat together with fresh spinach, creating a lighter yet protein‑rich meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “lasagna” comes from the Latin “laganum,” meaning “a flat strip.”
Traditional lasagna is made with beef, but poultry versions have become popular for their lower fat content.
Spinach not only adds a vibrant green color but also boosts iron and vitamin K levels.
In Italy there is a regional “Lasagna al Porco” made with pork; this poultry version is a healthier alternative.
The dish is often served in individual squares, making it convenient for family meals and gatherings.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Spinach supplies non‑heme iron, which is better absorbed when paired with vitamin C from tomato sauce.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Poultry contains less saturated fat than beef, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry meat and whole‑grain pasta deliver B6 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Parmesan and mozzarella add calcium important for bone health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauce and cheese are often high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Food‑borne bacteria risk
items.content: Undercooked poultry may harbor salmonella; ensure the meat reaches an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach is rich in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the lasagna hot, cut into portions. It pairs well with a light green salad or extra tomato sauce. Garnish with fresh basil or oregano for added aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion and freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed goat, Puerto Rican style is a traditional island dish made from tender pieces of goat meat slowly simmered in a fragrant sauce of tomatoes, paprika, garlic, onion, olive oil, and characteristic Puerto Rican spices such as adobo and cumin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Goat meat is considered a delicacy in Puerto Rico and is often served at family celebrations.
Long, low‑heat cooking makes the meat exceptionally tender and flavorful.
The sauce traditionally includes a hint of “piri‑piri” heat typical of Caribbean cuisine.
The dish is commonly accompanied by rice, beans, and fried plantains.
Fresh herbs like oregano and cilantro are added for a bright aromatic note.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Goat meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Compared with beef, goat meat generally contains less saturated fat, making it a heart‑friendlier option.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and healthy blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins source
items.content: Goat meat is a good source of vitamin B12 and niacin, which aid nerve health and metabolism.

items.title: Benefits from spices
items.content: Adobo, cumin, and garlic have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to goat meat, experiencing skin rashes or digestive reactions.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking can lead to salmonella or campylobacter contamination.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional sauces are often salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Caution with liver disease
items.content: Goat meat is relatively high in purines, which can raise uric acid levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot, typically with boiled rice, beans, and fried plantains. The meat can be shredded for tacos, burritos, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to at least 75 °C before serving.
